title: The Man Who Read the Stars
shortDescription: A shopkeeper's son from a village in East Bengal walked seven miles to school, lost a scholarship for a student boycott and wrote an equation at twenty-seven that changed how the world reads starlight. He also built an institute of nuclear physics in Calcutta, argued with Nehru and gave India its national calendar.
introduction: Seoratali, a village in the Dacca district of East Bengal, now Bangladesh. It is 1893, and a fifth child has been born into a shopkeeper's family. His father's grocery income is uncertain; his mother runs the house so well that no one in it feels deprived. The boy will walk seven miles to school, lose a scholarship for joining a student boycott, and write an equation at twenty-seven that changes how the world reads the light of stars. British intelligence will call him a revolutionary. He will build an institute of nuclear physics in Calcutta and argue with Nehru. His name is Meghnad Saha.

chapters.heading: The walk to school
paragraphs: The village was called Seoratali, in the Dacca district of East Bengal — a place now inside Bangladesh. Meghnad Saha was born there on 6 October 1893, the fifth of eight children of Jagannath Saha and Bhubaneswari Devi. His father kept a small grocery shop. The income was uncertain and the work constant. The family's authorised biography said they belonged to the Hindu middle class and had to work hard for a living; it rejected the idea of grinding poverty. The boy worked in the shop when he was not at his books. His mother managed the house so carefully that an early account said no one in it felt deprived.

School meant walking. The middle school at Simulia was seven miles away, and a local doctor, Ananta Kumar Das, gave him free board and lodging so he could attend. He carried flattened rice, chira, in the fold of his dhoti, and was proud of that walk for the rest of his life. At the village primary school he had learned to read and write; at Simulia he learned enough to sit an examination that would take him out of the district. In 1909 he sat the Calcutta University entrance examination and came first among all candidates from East Bengal.

Two years earlier a scholarship had taken him to the Government Collegiate School in Dacca. He had won it by standing first in the district's middle-school examination. Then the governor of Bengal, Bampfylde Fuller, came to visit. Saha joined the students who boycotted the visit, lost the scholarship and left the school. A private school, the Kishori Lal Jubilee School, gave him another. His daughter Chitra remembered the story from the other side: as a college student she was scolded for joining a procession, and her father told her he had once been expelled for leading a school boycott. He had not forgotten what it cost.

At Calcutta's Eden Hindu Hostel, meals were served separately for Brahmin and non-Brahmin boys. Saha's family belonged to a trading caste that Brahmins treated as socially lower, and he was once admonished for acting as priest at a Saraswati Puja. His daughter remembered that he cared little for urban sophistication and kept the broad accent of East Bengal all his life. The lesson of those hostel mealtimes was delivered daily: some doors were closed before a boy reached them.

chapters.heading: A bicycle across Calcutta
paragraphs: By 1911 he was at Dacca College, studying for the Intermediate Science examination. He came first in mathematics and chemistry and third in the examination as a whole. Three years later he took a BSc with honours in mathematics, placed second; the student above him was Satyendra Nath Bose, who would become his closest scientific companion. They were second and first again in the 1915 MSc in applied mathematics. In 1916 Saha became a lecturer in mathematics at the new University College of Science in Calcutta. A year later he and Bose moved together into physics.

He paid his way. Two or three private tuitions kept him going, and he cycled long distances across Calcutta between them. His salary, when it came, was about £150 a year, and he supported his parents and a younger brother from it. Then the colonial administration closed a different door: because of his nationalist associations he was refused permission to sit the Indian Finance Service examination. A government career was no longer available. The laboratory was.

In the years that followed he earned a doctorate for work on electromagnetic theory and radiation pressure, and won a research scholarship. In 1919 he and Bose produced the first English translation of Einstein's and Minkowski's papers on relativity — work that reached Calcutta while the world was still learning what those names meant. That same year the massacre at Jallianwala Bagh shook the country. Saha wrote that 'these incidents have degraded us before the whole world'. The man translating Einstein was also writing about national humiliation.

At the university he was already known as a teacher who prepared every lecture with care. Colleagues remembered the clear, bold handwriting on the blackboard, the lantern slides and the demonstration experiments laid out in front of the class. Kothari, who wrote his biographical memoir, called him a 'devoted and inspiring teacher' who 'gave his time generously'. Students did not forget a man like that. Nor did the men who ran the empire.

chapters.heading: The equation at twenty-seven
paragraphs: In 1919, while teaching thermodynamics and spectroscopy to M.Sc. students, Saha began to see a pattern in the light of the stars. A stellar spectrum is the barcode of a star's atmosphere: the dark lines in it are the fingerprints of atoms. Ionization is the process by which an atom loses an electron. Physicists could name the lines, but they could not explain why one star's spectrum showed calcium and another's did not. Saha's breakthrough was to connect the lines to temperature. He described the moment in a letter years later: 'It was while pondering over the problems of astrophysics, and teaching thermodynamics and spectroscopy to the M.Sc. classes that the theory of thermal ionization took a definite shape in my mind in 1919.'

A paper by the German physicist Eggert gave him the push. Saha saw the missing term — the ionization potential, the energy needed to strip an electron from an atom — and wrote that he 'thus arrived at the formula which now goes by my name'. Between February and September 1919 he prepared four papers and sent them from India to London. The central one appeared in the Philosophical Magazine in October 1920: 'Ionization in the solar chromosphere', pages 472 to 488 of volume 40. He was twenty-seven.

The equation linked temperature, pressure, ionization potential and the relative numbers of ionised and un-ionised atoms. With it, the sequence of stellar spectra became a temperature sequence rather than a catalogue of different ingredients. A star's light could be read as a measurement. In 1925 E. A. Milne wrote in Nature: 'Six years ago, practically no explanation existed of why some lines appear in stellar spectra and not others ... It is to Saha that we owe the key that has unlocked these mysteries.' Svein Rosseland put it more simply in 1936: 'The impetus given to astrophysics by Saha's work can scarcely be overestimated.'

The work was done in Calcutta, before he set foot in a British laboratory. When he wrote to H. H. Plaskett to settle the record, he said he had worked at Fowler's laboratory 'as a guest', had 'never registered my name as a scholar', and that the work 'had been mainly done in India before I went to Fowler's laboratory'. Plaskett answered in 1947: 'With the concept of thermal ionization your name will always be associated ... your place in history of the subject is secure for all time.'

chapters.heading: London, Berlin, Allahabad
paragraphs: Saha sailed to London in November 1920 and went to work in Alfred Fowler's spectroscopy laboratory at Imperial College. Fowler had read the Calcutta papers and suggested a new title for the work: 'On a physical theory of stellar spectra'. It appeared in the Proceedings of the Royal Society in 1921. Saha said the main ideas and the working had remained unchanged; only the presentation was recast. He also tried J. J. Thomson's Cavendish Laboratory, but found no apparatus there suited to what he wanted to do.

From February 1921 he worked in Walter Nernst's laboratory in Berlin. He returned to India in November. Calcutta University made him Khaira Professor, but there was little money for research. In 1923 Allahabad University made him its first professor and head of physics. His first lecture there was on 17 November. He walked into a department with almost no research tradition; the university refused even modest grants for apparatus. He built one anyway.

Saha's own memoir did not soften the place: there was 'practically no research atmosphere' at Allahabad. Yet the lectures were carefully prepared, the blackboard work bold and clear, and the demonstration experiments arranged for students to see. He stayed fifteen years, from 1923 to 1938, and taught a generation of Indian physicists how to ask questions of an instrument. In 1927, in the middle of those Allahabad years, he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society. One of the young men in his circle was B. D. Nagchaudhuri, who trained under Ernest Lawrence at Berkeley from 1938 and brought the idea of a cyclotron home.

In 1938 Saha returned to Calcutta as Palit Professor and kept the chair until 1953. The title mattered less than the work. He had spent years arguing for what India actually needed: academies, journals, money, and rooms where an experiment could survive a change of government.

chapters.heading: The ship called Henry
paragraphs: Saha's science never separated him from the politics of the country that produced him. In 1915 he moved in the circles of Anushilan Samiti, a revolutionary organisation in Bengal. He and Jadu Gopal Mukherjee were assigned to receive a consignment of arms from a German ship, the Henry. The arms were seized at Shanghai on 2 June. The ship returned to Germany on 22 June. Saha came back to Calcutta with nothing.

The colonial government had already closed the finance service to him. His daughter said he stayed anti-establishment under every government that followed, colonial or Indian. Years later, when he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1927 at the age of thirty-four, Sir James Jeans asked for a full report on him. What came back described Saha as 'a rabid revolutionary mixed up with various sorts of anti-British propaganda'. The accusation did not stop the election.

He was equally willing to argue with Indians. In 1938 he persuaded Subhas Chandra Bose to set up a National Planning Committee and then persuaded Nehru to chair it. In a letter to Nehru in August 1945 he criticised what he called 'old world ideologies — like spinning wheel and homespun', and argued for 'a decent living for India's masses' through the 'fullest use of science'. He wanted industry, electricity and instruments, and said so to men who did not always want to hear it.

His daughter remembered a man who acted on impulse, who could be abrasive and irritable, yet who would listen once he was convinced another person was right — 'and then he would appear so happy'. Friends found him outwardly 'remote, matter of fact, and even harsh' and, beneath that, capable of 'extreme warmth, deep humanity'. The combination made him a difficult colleague and an unforgettable one.

chapters.heading: A country of its own science
paragraphs: By the late 1920s Saha had turned from the interior of stars to the future of Indian science. In 1929 he published 'A Plea for an Academy of Sciences'. Two years later the Academy of Sciences of the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh was founded, with Saha as its first president, serving from 1931 to 1932. In the late 1930s he presided over the National Institute of Sciences of India, the body that became the Indian National Science Academy. He was also president of the Indian Physical Society in 1935.

In January 1934 he stood before the Indian Science Congress in Bombay as its general president. The address argued for a national academy that could bring 'a scientific handling of economic and industrial problems of the country'. In 1935 he began editing Science and Culture, a journal modelled on Nature, and edited it until his death. It gave Indian scientists a place to publish their own work and to argue about what that work was for.

In 1952 he became a member of Parliament and used the position to attack the secrecy of the Atomic Energy Commission. He had been writing about atomic energy in Science and Culture since 1939, and he pressed the government on its promise of a reactor. The man British intelligence had once called a rabid revolutionary was now asking awkward questions of an Indian government.

In November 1952 the government appointed him chairman of a Calendar Reform Committee. India used many calendars, with different eras and different starting points; the committee examined about thirty of them. Its report, published in 1955, recommended a single solar calendar in the Saka era. On 21 March 1956 that calendar took effect as 1 Chaitra 1878 Saka. A calendar is not usually counted as physics. He thought it was part of the same job.

chapters.heading: The building on Upper Circular Road
paragraphs: The institute Saha wanted took shape slowly. Calcutta University made land available at 92 Upper Circular Road in Rajabazar. In 1940 the Sir Dorabji Tata Charities Trust offered sixty thousand rupees, and the university agreed to match it. The Bengal government opposed the plan; B. C. Roy and Syamaprasad Mookerjee helped carry it through. On 21 April 1948 Mookerjee laid the foundation stone of the Institute of Nuclear Physics.

Money remained the hard part. Promised funds were delayed in 1948, fellowships went unpaid, and in 1949 Saha was asking for an advance of a lakh of rupees. Even a capital grant of three and a half lakh was not enough. He kept building. On 11 January 1950 the institute was formally opened by Madame Irène Joliot-Curie, the French physicist and Nobel laureate. That date is still its Foundation Day. It became autonomous in 1951 and was renamed the Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics after his death. He is recorded as its founder director.

A cyclotron was in the plans — a machine that uses a magnetic field to drive charged particles outward until they strike a target. Nagchaudhuri had been trained by Ernest Lawrence at Berkeley from 1938; the machine was commissioned in 1954, after Saha was gone. He did not live to see it turn on. The institute itself was his answer to the question that had followed him since the Allahabad days: how a poor country could do physics. He built the room, wrote the journal, trained the students and argued with the government.

He also gave the country a scientific press. Science and Culture carried his writing on atomic energy from 1939 onward. As a member of Parliament he attacked the Atomic Energy Commission for keeping too much of its work secret. The young man once denied a government post for his politics had become the man a government had to answer.

chapters.heading: What remains
paragraphs: In early January 1956 the foundation stone of a students' hall was laid at the institute by K. D. Malaviya. A few weeks later, on 16 February, Meghnad Saha died at the age of sixty-two. He left his wife Radha Rani, whom he had married in 1918, and seven children: Ajit, Ranjit, Prasenjit, Usha, Krishna, Chitra and Sanghamitra. His daughter remembered that nothing mattered to him as much as a happy family. The man who could be harsh in a committee room was, at home, simply a father.

The honours came in forms he would have understood. A crater on the far side of the Moon was named Saha by the International Astronomical Union in 1970, about a hundred and three kilometres across. India issued a commemorative stamp for his birth centenary on 23 December 1993. The institute in Rajabazar carries his name, and the academy he argued for became the Indian National Science Academy, which holds memorial lectures in his name.

The equation is the thing, though. Open a textbook on stellar spectra and the name appears in the index, attached to a relation between heat and the state of an atom. It was worked out in Calcutta in 1919 and published in 1920, when he was twenty-seven. It turned the light of a star into a measurement. It also carried the name of a shopkeeper's son from a village in East Bengal into textbooks around the world.

His daughter remembered the broad East Bengal accent, the chira in his dhoti on those long walks to school, and the pride he took in them. He once told a colleague, in his deadpan way, that he could not say whether P. C. Ray wanted a bullock cart to reach the station. The boy who walked seven miles to a middle school ended by giving his name to a crater on the Moon and a building where physicists study the nucleus. Between those two points lies the whole of a life.

sources.title: Biographical Memoir of Meghnad N. Saha (D. S. Kothari, 1960, Royal Society Biographical Memoirs v.5)
sources.note: Authoritative memoir. Supports the 6 October 1893 birth at Seoratali in Dacca district, the eight children and the shopkeeping father, the 1905 scholarship and loss of it over the governor's visit, the 1909 entrance result, 1911 and 1915 examinations, the private tuitions, the blocked finance-service exam, the 1919 translation of Einstein and Minkowski, the 1920 paper title and journal, the 1919 origin of the ionization theory, the 1921 Royal Society paper, the Allahabad appointment and its first lecture date, the Science Congress presidency, the Royal Society election in 1927 at thirty-four, and the teaching and personality descriptions.

sources.title: Meghnad Saha — letters, writings and reminiscences (2019 commemorative volume)
sources.note: Primary letters and family memoir. Supports the 6 October 1893 birth and the now-Bangladesh location, the family's rejection of an abject-poverty story, the grocery shop and uncertain income, the hostel's separate meals and the Saraswati Puja admonition, the daughter's account of the school boycott and of her father's temperament, the 1946 letter describing when the ionization theory took shape and the work done before Fowler's laboratory, the Plaskett correspondence and his 1947 reply, Milne's and Fowler's quoted tributes, the 1915 political associations, the 1927 intelligence report calling him a rabid revolutionary, the institute chronology, the wife and seven children, the 1956 students' hall and death date, and the bullock-cart anecdote.

sources.title: 'Meghnad Saha: Physicist and nationalist' (Somaditya Banerjee)
sources.note: Supports the 1915 Anushilan Samiti circles and the arms consignment from the ship Henry, its seizure at Shanghai on 2 June and the ship's return to Germany on 22 June; the 1905 expulsion; the 1919 relativity translation; the Jallianwala Bagh quotation; the significance of the equation in changing astronomical spectroscopy; Rosseland's 1936 tribute; the 1938 National Planning Committee; the 1945 letter to Nehru; and the account of Institute of Nuclear Physics funding. Note: this article wrongly says Marie Curie inaugurated the institute; the official institute history gives Irène Joliot-Curie.

sources.title: Meghnad Saha commemorative volume
sources.note: Supports the first professorship and headship of physics at Allahabad, the 1921 return from Europe, the National Planning Committee, the founding of Science and Culture in 1935, the outward harshness and inward warmth quoted in the story, the seven children, and the account of his final illness and death on 16 February 1956.
